record.title: chore: bootstrap multi-module Maven build
record.description:
Sets up the build every later slice lands in: four Maven modules with the dependency direction
fixed from the start.

- `core` — the domain and its ports, no Spring.
- `adapters` — persistence, the database clients and storage behind those ports.
- `application` — the use cases.
- `web` — the composition root and the console; the only module that sees both use cases and adapters.

Java 21, Spring Boot 4.1. `.gitignore` anchors `target/` to the build output so that a source
package called `target` is never ignored. ADR-001 records why the build is split this way.

`mvn verify` passes on the empty modules.

record.title: ci: add Maven verify and workflow lint
record.description:

  than letting a test skip itself.
- **workflow lint** — actionlint over `.github/workflows/`, so a broken workflow is caught in
  the pull request that breaks it.

`verify` becomes a required check on `develop` and `main` once this is merged.

record.title: feat(target): register and list MySQL targets (DBV-1)
record.description:
First vertical slice for DBV-1: an operator registers a MySQL database as a backup target and
sees the targets in a list.

- **Domain:** immutable `DatabaseTarget`; the password is encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a fresh
  12-byte IV per call, so two targets sharing a password do not share a ciphertext. Only the
  application layer holds the key.
- **Persistence:** JPA on PostgreSQL, Flyway migration `V1__database_targets.sql`. Name uniqueness
  is a functional unique index rather than a read-then-write check, which would lose the race
  between two concurrent registrations.
- **Web:** registration form and list page.
- **Tests:** unit tests for the domain and the use case, Testcontainers tests for the repository.
- **Docs:** ADR-002 on the password encryption.

No engine column yet: MySQL is the only engine, so the migration that adds a second one
introduces it.

record.title: feat(target): test the connection to a MySQL target (DBV-2)
record.description:
DBV-2: an operator can test a registered target before the first backup runs.

- The probe is `mysql --execute="SELECT 1"` rather than JDBC, so it exercises the same binaries and
  credential path a backup will use.
- MySQL's own error text is stored and shown verbatim: "Access denied for user" and "Can't connect
  to MySQL server" send an operator to different places, and a house-written "Connection failed"
  sends them nowhere.
- `ProcessRunner` concentrates the subprocess hazards: both pipes drained concurrently before
  `waitFor`, a timeout with `destroyForcibly`, secrets passed through the child's environment.
- `localhost` is rewritten to `127.0.0.1`: the client otherwise opens a Unix socket and ignores `--port`.
- Migration `V2__connection_check_results.sql`; the probe writes three columns through a targeted
  update, so it cannot rewrite the stored password. ADR-003 records the choice of the CLI client.

record.title: feat(backup): run a full logical MySQL backup (DBV-3)
record.description:
DBV-3: start a full logical backup of a MySQL target and see when it finished.

- Starting a backup persists a `RUNNING` row and commits it before submitting the work, so an
  accepted backup has a URL to poll before anything runs, and a crash leaves evidence instead of a
  lost in-memory task. Rows left `RUNNING` by a dead process are failed at startup.
- `mysqldump` writes the file itself, so a large schema never passes through the heap; a failed dump
  deletes its partial file before reporting, because a truncated dump restores as silent data loss.
- The worker pool is bounded on both axes, and a refusal is recorded as a failed execution.
- Removing a target that still has backups is refused rather than cascading.
- Migration `V3__backup_executions.sql`; a full-context integration test catches wiring problems the
  `@WebMvcTest` slices cannot see.

record.title: perf(backup): gzip the dump while it is written (DBV-4)
record.description:
DBV-4: backups of large databases filled the disk before compression started.

`mysqldump`'s stdout is now streamed through a `GZIPOutputStream` instead of being written with
`--result-file` and compressed afterwards. Memory is unchanged, since the copy goes through a fixed
buffer; peak disk use is the compressed size. An 18 MB schema compresses to 102 KB.

- `ProcessRunner.runStreaming` flushes the sink but never closes it: the gzip trailer is written on
  close, so everything that inspects or deletes the file happens after the adapter's
  try-with-resources block.
- If the sink cannot be written to (a full disk) the child is killed at once instead of blocking on
  an undrained pipe until the backup timeout.

ADR-006; supersedes the `--result-file` part of ADR-005.

record.title: feat(restore): restore a backup after explicit confirmation (DBV-5)
record.description:
DBV-5: restore a backup into its target, only after an explicit confirmation.

- The confirmation page requires the target's name to be typed: a checkbox is a reflex, and
  restoring into the wrong database is unrecoverable. It also says plainly that restore applies the
  dump and does not reset the schema; tables the backup does not contain are left alone.
- The archive is decompressed beside itself and the client's stdin is redirected from that file,
  so no thread of ours writes into a child that may itself be blocked writing output.
- `BackupStatus` becomes `ExecutionStatus`, shared with restores; the executor is shared too, so
  the bound is on total heavy work.
- Migration `V4__restore_executions.sql`, ADR-007, and the round-trip test this project exists for:
  seed, back up, drop the tables, restore, compare, quotes and non-ASCII included.

record.title: Delete backup artifacts from history
record.description:
Download a backup's archive, and delete a backup together with its file.

Deleting a backup removes its restore records, then its file, then its row. Row-first would, on a
failure to delete the file, strand an artifact on disk with nothing pointing at it. This way a
failure leaves a visible row whose file is already gone, and the operator can simply delete again.
The confirmation page counts the restore records that go with it.

Downloads serve the archive exactly as stored. Storage refuses to read or delete outside its root,
even for paths that came from the database. Deleting the backups is what finally makes a target
removable. ADR-008.

record.title: build: ship Docker image and compose quickstart (DBV-7)
record.description:
DBV-7: customers can try dbvault without building it.

- A two-stage `Dockerfile`: the build stage compiles the jar, the runtime stage carries a JRE, the
  jar and Ubuntu's `mysql-client` (Oracle MySQL 8.4). Debian's `default-mysql-client` is MariaDB,
  whose `mysqldump` rejects `--set-gtid-purged`, so every backup would fail.
- Runs as an unprivileged user, keeps artifacts in a named volume, and its healthcheck fetches a
  real page so it turns green only once Flyway has run.
- `docker-compose.yml` starts dbvault with its PostgreSQL metadata store; `docker compose up --build`
  needs nothing on the host but Docker.
- `docs/deployment.md` and ADR-009 explain what an operator has to decide.

record.title: feat(auth): single operator sign-in with CSRF protection (DBV-6)
record.description:
DBV-6: the console and the API are protected by one operator account configured at deployment.

**Console**
- Every page needs a signed-in operator, including paths that do not exist, so an anonymous visitor
  learns nothing about which do. The account comes from the environment: `OPERATOR_USERNAME` and a
  bcrypt `OPERATOR_PASSWORD_HASH` (ADR-011).
- CSRF tokens on every form; a form left open past the session gets "nothing was submitted" and a
  sign-in, not a bare 403. A strict Content-Security-Policy: fonts and scripts are self-hosted and
  no template carries inline script or style.
- Sign-in and sign-out are audited; the healthcheck moves to `/actuator/health`, which says UP or
  DOWN and nothing more.
- Smaller fixes found while testing the flow: a missing restore goes back to the restore list, a
  taken name or a target in use is refused before touching the database, times on the error page
  are UTC like the rest of the console.

**API for scripts and dbvault-cli**
- `GET /api/targets` and `GET /api/targets/{id}/backups`, read-only JSON, authenticated with HTTP
  Basic on every request against the same operator account; no session, no cookie.
- Responses leave out the password ciphertext and the artifact's path on disk; an unknown target is
  a JSON 404, an anonymous call a 401 rather than a redirect.

record.title: feat: list targets and backups (DBV-8)
record.description:
DBV-8: list targets and the backups of one target from the command line.

- `dbvault targets` prints id, name and address; `dbvault backups <target-id>` prints one target's
  backups newest first, with readable sizes.
- Both call the server's read-only `/api` (`GET /api/targets`, `GET /api/targets/{id}/backups`)
  with HTTP Basic on every request.
- The server address and username come from `~/.config/dbvault/cli.properties` (default
  `http://localhost:8090`, user `admin`); the password from `DBVAULT_PASSWORD`, or a prompt. It is
  never written to the file.
- Exit codes: `3` wrong credentials, `4` not found (with the server's message), `5` server unreachable.

Tested against a real HTTP server on a free port.

record.description:

- **A `v*` tag** builds the `Dockerfile` and pushes `ghcr.io/hoangtulangtoc/dbvault:<tag>` and `:latest`.

record.title: perf(restore): stream gunzip into the client (DBV-32)
record.description:
The archive is gunzipped as it is fed to mysql's stdin on a thread of its

archive still never reaches the target; a source that fails later kills
the client before its stdin is closed. Every pipe now has a dedicated
thread rather than one from the common pool, which two jobs could
exhaust on a small host. See ADR-016.

summaryWritten.whatChanged: Encryption of each target's password now uses a unique key derived from the master key via HKDF with the target's ID as context, instead of encrypting all passwords with the same key.
summaryWritten.whyChanged: To prevent a security vulnerability where leaking one master key and any ciphertext exposed all targets' credentials (DBV-16).
summaryWritten.technicalDetail: A new HKDF-SHA256 implementation derives per-target encryption keys. Old passwords decrypt as before and migrate to per-target keys on their next edit, while new passwords use the new format marked with a 'v2:' prefix. The master key or any per-target key alone can no longer decrypt all targets' credentials. `EncryptionPort` now provides 'encryptFor' and 'decryptFor', and all relevant flows use these methods.
summaryWritten.migrationStep: No direct action is required; credentials migrate to the new key scheme individually on update.

narratives.contributor: Passwords are now encrypted per target using keys derived from the master key via HKDF-SHA256, with 'encryptFor' and 'decryptFor' methods added to EncryptionPort. Existing password values remain compatible and are migrated to per-target keys upon update.
narratives.end_user: Your passwords are now better protected, as each one has its own encryption key. You don't need to do anything, and your data remains accessible.
narratives.operator: The encryption backend now uses per-target derived keys so that compromising the master key and a ciphertext exposes only one credential, not all. Credentials update to the new format when edited; monitor for any decryption issues during migration, but no global changes or rollback steps are necessary.

record.title: fix(crypto): derive per-target keys with HKDF (DBV-16)
record.description:
DBV-16: every target's password was encrypted with the one master key, so a single leaked
ciphertext-and-key pair exposed every target.

- `dev.dbvault.adapter.crypto.Hkdf` implements HKDF-SHA256 (RFC 5869, checked against its test
  vectors).
- Each target's password is now sealed under a key derived from the master key with the target's
  id as context. Values are prefixed `v2:`; one target's key does not open another's, and the master
  key alone opens neither.
- Passwords stored before this change still decrypt; they move to a per-target key the next time the
  password is edited. Storage profile secrets keep using the master key.
- `EncryptionPort` gains `encryptFor` / `decryptFor`; registration, edit, connection test, backup and
  restore use them.

record.title: feat(engine): MongoDB logical backup and restore (DBV-21)
record.description:
MongoDB becomes dbvault's third engine, next to MySQL and PostgreSQL. A MongoDB target is backed up with `mongodump` into one gzipped archive and restored with `mongorestore`, through the same backup and restore flows as the SQL engines.

What changes:

* A target has an optional **authentication database**. It is required for MongoDB (the console defaults it to `admin`), refused for MySQL and PostgreSQL, and can be edited later. Migration `V11` adds the column and widens the engine check; existing rows are untouched.
* Connection test runs `mongodump` against a random, absent collection, so it proves the host, port and credentials without reading operator data.
* Backup writes one `.archive.gz` artifact with `--archive --gzip --db`. Restore does a `--dryRun` first, then `--drop --stopOnError` with `--nsFrom/--nsTo`, so an archive can be restored into another registered MongoDB database.
* The password never appears in process arguments: each tool call gets a 0600 YAML config file that is deleted as soon as the process ends.
* The image and CI install MongoDB Database Tools (`mongodump`, `mongorestore`); the application refuses to start without them, like the SQL clients. The adapters reuse the shared `ClientBinaries` check.
* ADR-018 records the decisions.

Limits, on purpose: one host and port with SCRAM user/password only (no URI, replica-set seed list, SRV, TLS or external auth); a dump taken while writes continue is not a point-in-time snapshot; a restore that fails part-way may already have replaced some collections, and its record says so.

How to verify: `mvn verify` runs the MongoDB adapters against a real MongoDB in Testcontainers, including a restore into a second database.

record.title: feat(notify): Slack, email and webhook channels (DBV-22)
record.description:
Operators can now be told when a backup or restore starts, succeeds or fails, without watching the console. Destinations are reusable **notification channels**; each target picks which channels it uses and for which events.

What changes:

* A new **Notifications** page manages channels of three types: Slack (incoming webhook, official `hooks.slack.com` HTTPS hosts only), Email (recipient per channel; SMTP is configured once for the deployment) and a generic Webhook (HTTP or HTTPS, with a stable JSON body). **Send test** makes a real delivery and records the result.
* Each target has a notifications tab: choose channels and any of the six events (backup or restore started, succeeded, failed). A new subscription starts with the two failure events.
* Slack and webhook URLs are encrypted at rest with `ENCRYPTION_SECRET_KEY` and never shown again; leaving the field empty on edit keeps the stored one. A channel's type cannot change after it is created.
* Events are sent after the execution row is stored: `STARTED` before the engine client runs, then exactly one success or failure. Queue rejection and the startup repair of interrupted backups send a failure too. A restore uses the destination target's subscriptions; the message names both targets.
* Delivery is best-effort: a failing channel is logged and the others are still tried; nothing about notifications can change a backup's or restore's result. There is no retry or outbox. HTTP calls time out after 3 s to connect and 5 s per request; SMTP after 5 s. Passwords, tokens and credentials in URLs are redacted before an error message reaches a channel.
* Migration `V12` adds the channel and subscription tables. Deleting a target removes its subscriptions; deleting a channel is refused while a target still uses it.
* `docker-compose.yml` gains the optional `DBVAULT_SMTP_*` settings. ADR-028 records the decisions.

How to verify: `mvn verify`; then in the console add a Webhook channel pointing at any request bin, press Send test, subscribe a target and run a backup.

record.title: feat(verify): isolated restore verification (DBV-23)
record.description:
A checksum proves an artifact still holds the bytes the backup wrote; it does not prove the engine can restore them. This adds **restore verification**: a backup is restored into a throwaway database that exists only for that check, inspected, and thrown away — never into one of the operator's targets.

What changes:

* The backup detail page gets **Test restore** next to **Verify checksum**, with the history of every attempt. A target can also opt into **verify after every successful backup**.
* Each attempt is its own record (`RUNNING` → `SUCCEEDED` or `FAILED`) attached to one successful backup; attempts can be repeated, and at most one runs at a time for a backup. A verification failure never changes the backup's result, its retention, or its notifications.
* The artifact is materialised (local or S3) and its SHA-256 checked first. MySQL (`mysql:8.4`), PostgreSQL (`postgres:17-alpine`) and MongoDB (`mongo:8.0`) are each restored into a container with no published port and a name derived from the attempt, then checked: `CHECK TABLE` on every MySQL table, a read of every PostgreSQL user table, `validate` on every MongoDB collection. Success is stored only after the container has been removed. The source target's credentials are never used.
* Pull, startup, check and cleanup all have timeouts; attempts left running when the application stops are marked failed on startup and their container removed.
* New notification events `VERIFICATION_SUCCESS` and `VERIFICATION_FAILED`; a newly selected channel defaults to the backup, restore and verification failure events.
* Migration `V13` adds `database_targets.verify_after_backup` and `restore_verification_executions`.
* It is **off by default** (`DBVAULT_VERIFICATION_ENABLED=false`). Turning it on needs the host Docker socket, which is root-equivalent access to the host, so `docker-compose.yml` leaves the socket mount commented out and the image only carries the Docker CLI. ADR-029 records the decisions.

Also drops three leftover `dbvault.mariadb.*`/`dbvault.sqlite.*` test properties and corrects the notification adapter count in the architecture overview (both from the previous PR).

How to verify: `mvn verify` restores real backups into disposable MySQL, PostgreSQL and MongoDB containers, including a corrupt archive that must fail and leave no container behind.

record.title: feat: add verify command (DBV-26)
record.description:
`dbvault verify` starts a restore verification of one backup on the server and waits for the outcome, so a script or a cron job can tell whether its backups actually restore (DBV-26).

What changes:

* `dbvault verify --backup-id <id> [--timeout PT30M]` calls `POST /api/v1/backups/{id}/verifications`, then follows the attempt every two seconds until it is no longer running, and prints the result.
* The exit code is the outcome: `0` it restored and passed its checks, `8` it failed (with the server's reason), `6` the server would not start it (verification disabled, unsupported or unavailable), `9` still running at the timeout — it carries on on the server.
* Every command now calls `/api/v1`. dbvault 0.3 moved the API there and drops the unversioned paths, so this client needs a 0.3 server; 0.2 servers are not supported any more.
* README lists the command and the new exit codes.

How to verify: `mvn verify` — `ServerCommandsTest` runs the commands against a local HTTP server, including a verification that succeeds after two polls, one that fails, one the server refuses, and a timeout.

record.title: feat(api): version the HTTP API under /api/v1 (DBV-24)
record.description:
The HTTP API moves under `/api/v1`, so it can grow and later change shape without breaking every client at once (DBV-24). Version 1 is what `/api` served, plus the restore verification that dbvault-cli needs next (DBV-26).

What changes:

* `GET /api/v1/targets` and `GET /api/v1/targets/{id}/backups` replace `/api/targets…`, with the same JSON.
* New: `POST /api/v1/backups/{id}/verifications` starts a test restore of one backup and answers `202` with the attempt and a `Location` to follow; `GET /api/v1/verifications/{id}` reports it (`RUNNING`, `SUCCEEDED` or `FAILED`). A verification that cannot start (disabled for the deployment, unsupported, unavailable, or a backup that did not succeed) is `409` with the reason.
* The old `/api/targets…` paths now answer `308 Permanent Redirect` to the same path under `/api/v1`, with `Deprecation: true` and a `successor-version` link. They still need credentials.
* The API's security chain no longer asks for a CSRF token. It creates no session and reads no cookie — every request carries its own HTTP Basic credentials — so there is nothing for a forged request to ride on. The console keeps CSRF protection.
* `docs/api.md` documents the API; ADR-039 records the versioning rule.

BREAKING CHANGE: the API now lives under `/api/v1`. The unversioned `/api/targets` paths only redirect there (`308`) and will be removed before 0.3.0 ships; scripts and clients that do not follow redirects — dbvault-cli 0.2 included — must call `/api/v1` themselves.

How to verify: `mvn verify`; `curl -u admin -i http://localhost:8080/api/targets` shows the `308` and its `Location`.

record.title: fix(schedule): handle daylight saving gaps in cron schedules (DBV-25)
record.description:
A schedule whose time falls in the hour a zone skips in spring never ran that day (DBV-25). `0 30 2 * * ?` in `America/New_York` had no run on 2026-03-08, when the clocks jump from 02:00 to 03:00; the same in `Europe/Berlin` on 2026-03-29. That is Quartz's own cron trigger: a wall-clock time that does not exist is skipped.

What changes:

* Schedules use a small `WallClockCronTrigger` instead of Quartz's builder-made cron trigger. The expression is matched against wall-clock time in the schedule's zone, then placed in the zone like `java.time` does: a time the zone skips runs as far into the day as the jump (02:30 → 03:30), and a time the autumn change repeats runs once, at its first occurrence.
* Only `getFireTimeAfter` is overridden. Quartz uses it for the first fire, after every fire and after a misfire, so the existing "do nothing" misfire rule and the next-run shown in the console are unchanged.
* The autumn case was checked as well: Quartz already ran a repeated time only once (at its second occurrence); it now runs at the first, and a restart inside the repeated hour does not run the day again.
* ADR-023 describes the rule.

How to verify: `WallClockCronTriggerTest` walks the 2026 spring and autumn changes in New York and Berlin, a restart inside the repeated hour, and an ordinary day in a zone without daylight saving.

record.title: fix(schedule): handle daylight saving gaps in cron schedules (DBV-25)
record.description:
A schedule whose time falls in the hour a zone skips in spring never ran that day (DBV-25). `0 30 2 * * ?` in `America/New_York` had no run on 2026-03-08, when the clocks jump from 02:00 to 03:00; the same in `Europe/Berlin` on 2026-03-29. That is Quartz's own cron trigger: a wall-clock time that does not exist is skipped.

What changes:

* Schedules use a small `WallClockCronTrigger` instead of Quartz's builder-made cron trigger. The expression is matched against wall-clock time in the schedule's zone, then placed in the zone like `java.time` does: a time the zone skips runs as far into the day as the jump (02:30 → 03:30), and a time the autumn change repeats runs once, at its first occurrence.
* Only `getFireTimeAfter` is overridden. Quartz uses it for the first fire, after every fire and after a misfire, so the existing "do nothing" misfire rule and the next-run shown in the console are unchanged.
* The autumn case was checked as well: Quartz already ran a repeated time only once (at its second occurrence); it now runs at the first, and a restart inside the repeated hour does not run the day again.
* ADR-023 describes the rule.

How to verify: `WallClockCronTriggerTest` walks the 2026 spring and autumn changes in New York and Berlin, a restart inside the repeated hour, and an ordinary day in a zone without daylight saving.

record.title: feat(observability): Prometheus metrics and Grafana dashboard (DBV-30)
record.description:
Operators can now watch their backups from Prometheus and Grafana (DBV-30).

What changes:

* `/actuator/prometheus` serves the backup metrics, one series per target (tags `target` and `engine`):
  * `dbvault_backup_last_success_timestamp_seconds`, `dbvault_backup_last_duration_seconds`, `dbvault_backup_last_size_bytes` — of the target's newest successful backup;
  * `dbvault_backup_failures_24h` — its backups that failed in the last 24 hours.
* The values are read from the execution history every 30 seconds on a background thread, so a scrape never waits on the database and a restart loses nothing; they say what the console says. A removed target drops out at the next refresh.
* The scrape uses the API's security chain: HTTP Basic with the operator account, no session, like dbvault-cli. `/actuator/health` is unchanged (public, UP or DOWN only).
* An optional `observability` compose profile runs Prometheus (v3.14.0) and Grafana (13.2.1), both pinned by digest, with a provisioned **dbvault backups** dashboard: failed backups in the last 24 hours, time since the last success per target, duration and size per target. Neither publishes a port. Their two passwords come from files the operator writes (both git-ignored), so a plain `docker compose up` still needs nothing new.
* `docs/deployment.md` explains it; ADR-040 records why the metrics come from the history rather than from in-memory counters.

How to verify: `mvn verify` (`BackupMetricsTest`; `DbvaultApplicationIT` scrapes the endpoint without and with credentials). With compose: write the two password files, `docker compose --profile observability up -d`, map Grafana's port in an override, open the dashboard.

summaryWritten.whatChanged: Database target connections now require TLS encryption by default, with an explicit opt-out per target. Existing targets will fail to connect if their server does not support TLS after upgrade, unless explicitly configured otherwise. API, configuration, migration logic, test coverage, and documentation have been updated to reflect and enforce this new default requirement.
summaryWritten.whyChanged: Previously, database credentials and dumps could be transmitted in plaintext due to default client behavior; this change enforces encryption to prevent data from crossing the network unencrypted, reducing the risk of credential exposure and interception.
summaryWritten.technicalDetail: A new field `tls_required` (default TRUE) is added to `database_targets`, enforced in API, configuration forms, backup/restore command lines (e.g., `--ssl-mode=REQUIRED` for MySQL, `PGSSLMODE=require` for PostgreSQL, `--tls` for MongoDB), and documented in ADR-041 and deployment docs. Tests are updated to require TLS where available. Opting out sets clients to prefer but not require TLS; warnings are shown where TLS is not enforced. Migration V14 sets up DB schema changes. Server certificate validation is not enforced yet except for MongoDB, which requires certificates match system CA.
summaryWritten.migrationStep: After upgrade, DBAs must verify every target: servers must support TLS or each affected target must opt out by clearing 'Require TLS'. Targets that cannot establish TLS will fail connection tests and backups until resolved.

record.title: security: enforce TLS to database targets (DBV-33)
record.description:
Every connection to a database target is now encrypted unless the target opts out (DBV-33). Until now each client's default decided: the MySQL client and libpq fall back to plain text without a word when a server does not offer TLS, and the MongoDB tools never encrypt unless asked — so a target's password and its whole dump could cross the network in clear text, and nothing said so.

What changes:

* A target has **Require TLS for every connection**, ticked by default. Backups, restores and connection tests then refuse a server that will not encrypt:
  * MySQL (`mysql`, `mysqldump`): `--ssl-mode=REQUIRED`;
  * PostgreSQL (`psql`, `pg_dump`, `pg_restore`): `PGSSLMODE=require`;
  * MongoDB (`mongodump`, `mongorestore`): `--tls`.
* Clearing the box is the opt-out for a server that cannot speak TLS. The clients are then told `--ssl-mode=PREFERRED` / `PGSSLMODE=prefer` explicitly (MongoDB gets no TLS option), so an option file on the host cannot decide for the target. The target list marks it **TLS not required**, and its edit form warns while it stays that way. Changing the setting drops the last connection check.
* `GET /api/v1/targets` includes `tlsRequired`.
* Migration `V14` adds `database_targets.tls_required`, default `TRUE`.
* Restore verification is unchanged: its throwaway containers are not reached over the network.
* ADR-041 records the decision and its limits; `docs/deployment.md` and `docs/api.md` describe it.

Required means encrypted, not authenticated: `REQUIRED`/`require` accept any certificate, including the one MySQL 8 generates for itself. Checking the server's identity needs a CA per target and is left for later. MongoDB's `--tls` does check the certificate against the image's CA store, so a MongoDB server with a self-signed certificate has to be opted out for now.

BREAKING CHANGE: existing targets require TLS after the upgrade. A server that does not offer TLS fails its next connection test and backup until it is given TLS or its target's **Require TLS** box is cleared.

How to verify: `mvn verify`. The MySQL integration tests now run with TLS required against MySQL 8.4 and check the session's `Ssl_cipher`; the PostgreSQL and MongoDB test containers do not speak TLS, so those tests opt out.

record.title: chore(legal): add third-party licence report
record.description:
The application jar now says what it bundles: every third-party library in it, with the licence that library declares, written by the build into `THIRD-PARTY.txt`.

What changes:

* `license-maven-plugin` 2.7.1 (`add-third-party`, `generate-resources` of `web`) writes the report from the dependencies' own POMs; it lands at `BOOT-INF/classes/THIRD-PARTY.txt` in the jar, so the list always matches the jar it ships in. 172 libraries today.
* Runtime and compile dependencies only. dbvault's own modules are left out — their POMs inherit Spring Boot's `<licenses>` from the parent, which is not a licence dbvault has chosen — and so is Lombok, which is not packaged. The plugin's `excludedGroups` does not drop reactor modules, so a small template (`web/src/license/THIRD-PARTY.ftl`) does.
* A dependency that declares no licence fails the build (`failOnMissing`). Spellings of one licence are merged, and a library that offers a choice lists every licence it names (Logback: EPL 2.0 or LGPL 2.1; the Jakarta APIs: EPL 2.0 or GPL 2 with the Classpath Exception).
* `docs/licences.md` explains the report and what it does not cover (the client tools in the image, the fonts in `NOTICE`); `NOTICE` points to it.

No change to the application's behaviour. How to verify: `mvn verify` (`ThirdPartyReportTest`); `unzip -p web/target/web-*.jar BOOT-INF/classes/THIRD-PARTY.txt`.

record.title: fix: reject a server address that is not an http(s) URL (DBV-44)
record.description:
A server address the HTTP client cannot call no longer ends in an internal error (DBV-44).

* `DBVAULT_URL=localhost:8090` (no scheme) used to be read as the scheme `localhost`, and a `server=` line that is not a URL made `URI.create` throw: either way every command ended with exit code `1` and no hint.
* The address must now be `http://` or `https://` with a host. Otherwise the command stops with exit code `2` and says which setting is wrong — `DBVAULT_URL`, or `server in <file>` — and the form it expects.

How to verify: `mvn verify` (two new tests in `ServerCommandsTest`); `DBVAULT_URL=localhost:8090 dbvault targets; echo $?` prints the message and `2`.

record.title: build(docker): pin base images by digest
record.description:
Pins every container image dbvault builds from or runs by digest (OPS-13), so a rebuild gets the same bytes until a reviewed pull request changes them.

* `Dockerfile`: the build stage (`maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21`), the Docker CLI stage (`docker:27.5.1-cli`) and the runtime (`eclipse-temurin:21-jre-noble`) each name the multi-platform index digest beside their tag.
* `docker-compose.yml`: `postgres:17-alpine` is pinned too; Prometheus and Grafana already were.
* `.github/dependabot.yml` gains the `docker` and `docker-compose` ecosystems, weekly into `develop` like the others, so a new digest arrives as a `dependencies` pull request instead of silently on the next build.
* `docs/deployment.md` says so beside the note on the base image's seven binaries.

How to verify: `docker build .`, then in the image `command -v` finds `mysqldump mysql psql pg_dump pg_restore mongodump mongorestore` (checked: all seven, user `dbvault`).

record.title: test(mongo): wait for the final server and pin the image
record.description:
`MongoBackupRestoreIT` failed on most CI runs since `mongo:8.0` moved to 8.0.34 (17 Oct): `container … is not running` on the runners, `ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:27017` locally once the new image was pulled.

Two causes, two changes (test only):

* **Readiness probed the wrong server.** The official image creates the root user with a bootstrap `mongod`, then stops it and starts the real one. The probe asked loopback, which the bootstrap server answers too, so "stable for two seconds" could be the bootstrap server, which then stopped under the first test. It now probes through the container's own hostname: the bootstrap server binds `127.0.0.1` only (`--bind_ip 127.0.0.1` in the entrypoint), the real one `--bind_ip_all`.
* **8.0.34 exits on the runners.** Even probing the right server, the 8.0.34 container stopped during startup on GitHub's runners (it runs locally). The test now pins `mongo:8.0.32` by digest, like every other image since OPS-13; a later 8.0 can replace it once a CI run shows it stays up. When the server never comes up, the failure now carries the container's own log.

How to verify: `mvn -pl adapters -am clean verify -Dit.test=MongoBackupRestoreIT` — passed three times out of three locally, after failing with the floating tag.

record.title: feat(ui): finish the Vietnamese console (DBV-31)
record.description:
Second and last part of the Vietnamese console (DBV-31): every console page now reads in English or Vietnamese, with the choice per browser that the first part introduced.

What changes:

* Translated: storage, notification channels and per-target subscriptions, schedules, retention, backup detail and deletion (one or several), restores (list, confirmation, detail), target removal, the error page, and the shared confirmation dialog.
* Flash messages come from the bundles in the language of the request that set them (`ConsoleText`, a `MessageSource` lookup). Form checks use `{key}` in their annotations, resolved through the same bundles; the subscription check's code `notification.events` has its own line.
* The live job follower in `app.js` no longer carries sentences: the backup and restore pages render them into `data-live-*` attributes, as ADR-042 asks of scripts.
* Patterns with arguments go through `MessageFormat`, so a quote is written twice; a new test formats every such pattern in both bundles. Byte counts use `{0,number,#}` and keep their exact figure. The English wording is unchanged, so the existing controller tests still read the same sentences; four assertions now expect the number inside the sentence instead of a separate `<span>`.
* Still English by design: the HTTP API, CLI, logs, notifications, and the reason a domain rule or a database client gives for refusing something. ADR-042 and `docs/deployment.md` say so.

How to verify: `mvn verify` (`ConsoleLanguageTest`: a form check and a flash message in Vietnamese, every pattern formats, both bundles have the same keys); open `/schedules?lang=vi`, `/restores`, `/storage`, an error page, and submit an empty target form.

narratives.contributor: Internationalization has been added for Vietnamese. All English UI elements are now also available in Vietnamese. The language is selectable by the operator, requiring translation coverage for future additions. No code changes required for existing customizations unless they interact with locale handling.
narratives.dba: This change affects only the console's display language and does not alter database contents, schema, credentials, or backup/restore workflows. No DBA action or verification is required for upgrade or rollback.
narratives.end_user: You can now use the console in Vietnamese as well as English. Choose the language you prefer when using the console.
narratives.operator: After deployment, operators can select Vietnamese in the console. No operational risk or rollback steps are introduced; monitor user reports for any translation or language selection issues.
